pass_b_english: People often oppose those who grieve and resist their enemies with equal anger, but when it comes to children, they spare them; however, they take pleasure in human blood and gaze upon the altars of the gods with delight, considering it a delight to sacrifice human beings.
According to Julian, they have this tendency naturally, as he says.
Someone might say that we are merely playing with words by intending to imply a criminology in those things, for it is not as if such things had ever happened to men.
Let us examine, therefore, from the Greek historians, whether they did not indeed pollute their altars and temples with human blood and sacrifices.

Aristomenes the Messenian was grateful to Jupiter for the three hundred dead bodies, and he was also grateful to the Lacedaemonian kings, and this one added the king, and from there the highest and greatest of the gods, and the prince of the gods, who pitied the wretched and saw their full altar.

It was a custom for men to make their own misfortunes a delight, and the Scythians, who lived around the Tauric Chersonese, would intercept and kill strangers and hang their heads on the temple doors as an offering to the goddess, and they would bring her human slaughter as a gift.
To them, it would seem more cruel to snatch away the hope of salvation from those who had escaped, merely showing the pretext of death.

Erechtheus of the Athenians, having been approached by subterranean daemons, is said to have cruelly slaughtered his own daughter, as Dorotheus, a historian, reports in the fourth book of his histories.
Monymus also reports, in the collection of wonders, the immolation of Peleus and Chiron in the city of Pellene in Thrace, and that the altar of Dionysus in Lesbos was imbued with the blood of men.
While the pagan superstition was still strong, gladiatorial contests were held at Rome, and some were hidden under the earth with perforated stones, so that the blood of the fallen would pollute.

Porphyry writes in his second book about abstaining from animate things, thus: 'History is about not only what Theophrastus remembered, but also many other things, that humans were sacrificed.', and this is fully recorded in history.
For in Rhodes, in the month of Meta, on the sixth day, a human was sacrificed to Agraulos, the daughter of Cecrops and the nymph Agraulis, in the city of Salamis, which was previously called Coronis.
This custom continued until the time of Diomedes, when it was changed, and a temple of Minerva was built, and the sacrifice of humans to Agraulos and Diomedes was stopped.

Furthermore, the one to be immolated, who was from Athens and Agra, and who was led by ephebes, went around the altar three times; then the priest struck him with a knife in the stomach, and the pyre was set on fire, burning him completely.

They also sacrificed humans in Chios and Tenedos, and the Phoenicians sacrificed humans to Saturn, saying that the slaughter of humans was a sacrifice to the gods, but it was not to the gods, rather to the evil demons.

The Cretans, on the other hand, sacrificed the Curetes to Cronus, and the altars of the gods were polluted with the blood of miserable humans, which the Greeks believed was a delight for them, but not for the gods, rather for the evil demons.

They would place Saturn and Jupiter and Mars and the sister of Castor, and they would rejoice in the stupid Bacchus and the sister of Apollo, and they would worship them, showing that they were actually worshiping evil demons, not the gods.
